title: Placental Abruption -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Placental abruption, the premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall before completion of the second stage of labor, is a rare but serious complication of pregnancy. Occurring in approximately 0.4% to 1.0% of pregnancies, it is a leading cause of bleeding in the second half of gestation and poses significant risks, including maternal hemorrhage, morbidity, mortality, and fetal compromise or death. The sudden and unpredictable onset of placental abruption necessitates rapid recognition and intervention to preserve both maternal and fetal health.

title: Placental Abruption -- Continuing Education Activity
content: This activity equips clinicians with the knowledge and tools needed to address the challenges of placental abruption. Participants review the pathophysiology, epidemiology, diagnostic complexities, and evidence-based treatment strategies associated with this condition. The activity also emphasizes the importance of efficient evaluation, prompt stabilization, and effective interprofessional collaboration. By engaging in this activity, clinicians can expect to enhance their ability to identify, manage, and coordinate care for patients experiencing placental abruption, ultimately improving maternal and neonatal outcomes.

title: Placental Abruption -- Introduction
content: Placental abruption is the early separation of a placenta from the lining of the uterus before the completion of the second stage of labor. This condition is a leading cause of bleeding during the second half of pregnancy. Placental abruption is a relatively rare but serious complication of pregnancy that puts the well-being of both mother and fetus at risk. This condition is also known as abruptio placentae (see Image. Placental Abruption). [1] [2]

title: Placental Abruption -- Etiology
content: The exact etiology of placental abruption is unknown. However, many factors are associated with its occurrence. Risk factors can be categorized into 3 categories—health history, including behaviors and past obstetrical events; current pregnancy factors; and physical trauma. Health history factors that increase the risk of placental abruption include smoking, cocaine use during pregnancy, age older than 35, hypertension, and placental abruption in a prior pregnancy. Conditions specific to the current pregnancy that are associated with increased placental abruption risk are multiple gestation pregnancies, polyhydramnios, preeclampsia, sudden uterine decompression, and a short umbilical cord. Finally, abdominal trauma—such as that caused by a motor vehicle accident, fall, or physical assault—can lead to placental abruption.

title: Placental Abruption -- Etiology
content: Placental abruption occurs when there is a compromise of the vascular structures supporting the placenta. In other words, the vascular networks connecting the uterine lining and the maternal side of the placenta are disrupted. These vascular structures deliver oxygen and nutrients to the fetus. Disruption of the vascular network may occur in the setting of hypertension, substance use, or conditions that cause distention of the uterus. The uterus is a muscle and is elastic, whereas the placenta is comprised of epithelial, connective, and vascular tissue and thus less elastic than the uterus. Therefore, when the uterine tissue stretches suddenly, the vascular structure connecting the uterine wall to the placenta tears away. [3] [4]

title: Placental Abruption -- Epidemiology
content: Placental abruption is an uncommon but serious complication, occurring in approximately 0.4% to 1.0% of pregnancies, and often requires emergent management. [5] Most cases develop before 37 weeks of gestation and contribute significantly to maternal morbidity and perinatal mortality. [6] [7] Affected individuals are at risk for severe hemorrhage, blood transfusion, hysterectomy, coagulopathies such as disseminated intravascular coagulation, renal failure, and even death. [8] Substantial blood loss may also lead to Sheehan syndrome, or postpartum pituitary necrosis. Notably, about 70% of patients are classified as low risk, underscoring the difficulty of predicting placental abruption based solely on known risk factors. [9]

title: Placental Abruption -- Epidemiology
content: With the availability of blood replacement, maternal death resulting from placental abruption is rare but continues to be a significant contributor to the overall maternal mortality rate. Neonatal consequences include preterm birth and low birth weight, perinatal asphyxia, stillbirth, and neonatal death. In many countries, the rate of placental abruption has been increasing, even with improved obstetrical care and monitoring techniques. This paradox suggests a multifactorial etiology that is not well understood. [10] [3]

title: Placental Abruption -- Pathophysiology
content: Placental abruption occurs when the maternal vessels tear away from the placenta, and bleeding occurs between the uterine lining and the maternal side of the placenta. As the blood accumulates, it further separates the uterine wall and placenta. The placenta is the fetus's source of oxygen and nutrients, as well as the way the fetus excretes waste products. Diffusion to and from the maternal circulatory system is essential to maintaining these life-sustaining functions of the placenta. When blood accumulation causes the separation of the placenta from the maternal vascular network, these vital functions of the placenta are interrupted. If the fetus does not receive enough oxygen and nutrients, stillbirth can result. [11] [12]

title: Placental Abruption -- Histopathology
content: Once the placenta is delivered, a retroplacental clot is almost always observed. In some cases, there may be evidence of blood extravasation into the myometrium, resulting in purple discoloration of the uterus's serosa.

title: Placental Abruption -- History and Physical
content: Placental abruption is a leading cause of vaginal bleeding in the second half of pregnancy. Obtaining a detailed history and performing a thorough physical examination are essential to distinguish placental abruption from other causes of vaginal bleeding. Because a definitive diagnosis of placental abruption can only be made after birth, when the placenta is examined, obtaining a detailed history and performing a thorough physical examination are critical to the appropriate management of the maternal-fetal dyad. Placental abruption is a potentially life-threatening situation. Therefore, accurate patient assessment is essential to developing a proper management plan and preventing a possible poor outcome.

title: Placental Abruption -- History and Physical
content: The history should begin with a review of the prenatal course, focusing on the placental location in prior sonograms and any history of placental abruption in previous pregnancies. The clinician should inquire about the time of onset, the volume of bleeding, and any associated symptoms, such as cramping and abdominal pain. Exploring the pregnant person's behaviors, specifically whether they smoke or use cocaine, is a critical component of history. Asking about physical trauma, especially in the abdominal area, needs to be tactful and supportive. In cases of partner abuse, the pregnant individual may be hesitant to disclose that abdominal trauma has occurred.

title: Placental Abruption -- History and Physical
content: An assessment of the patient is the most useful mechanism for recognizing the onset of placental abruption. Vital signs should be obtained and reviewed, as tachycardia or hypotension may be indicators of hypovolemia from hemorrhage, which can be concealed. The physical examination includes palpation of the uterus. The gravid uterus is palpated for tenderness, consistency, and frequency and duration of uterine contractions. A sterile speculum examination should be performed to assess the cervix and to evaluate for the presence of bleeding. If the placental location is not known from prior sonograms, a digital examination of the cervix should be delayed until a sonogram is obtained for placental location and to rule out a placenta previa. If bleeding is present, the quantity and characteristics of the blood, as well as the presence of clots, should be noted. The absence of vaginal bleeding does not eliminate the diagnosis of placental abruption.

title: Placental Abruption -- History and Physical
content: Evaluation of fetal well-being is an essential component of the assessment. The examination should begin with auscultation of fetal heart sounds and inquiry about fetal movement, with attention to any recent changes in activity. For pregnancies at or beyond viability, continuous electronic fetal monitoring is recommended to detect prolonged bradycardia, reduced variability, or late decelerations. In pregnancies before viability, Doppler assessment to confirm the presence of fetal heart tones is sufficient.

title: Placental Abruption -- Evaluation
content: There are no laboratory tests or diagnostic procedures to definitively diagnose placental abruption. However, some studies may be conducted to eliminate other conditions and provide baseline data. [13] [14] [15]
contents: Placental Abruption -- Evaluation. There are no laboratory tests or diagnostic procedures to definitively diagnose placental abruption. However, some studies may be conducted to eliminate other conditions and provide baseline data. [13] [14] [15]

title: Placental Abruption -- Evaluation -- An ultrasound examination helps determine the location of the placenta and rule out the diagnosis of placenta previa. However, ultrasound's sensitivity in visualizing placental abruption is low. During the acute phase of placental abruption, the hemorrhage is isoechoic or similar to the surrounding placental tissue. Therefore, visualization and differentiation of the concealed hemorrhage associated with placental abruption from the surrounding placental tissue are difficult. The diagnosis of placental abruption cannot be confirmed or discarded based solely on an ultrasound.
content: The fetal heart tracing is an essential component of the evaluation when abruption is suspected. Although it cannot definitively rule in or out an abruption, fetal heart tracing is a helpful tool in assessing the status of the pregnant individual and fetus. Although a comprehensive review of fetal heart tracings is beyond the scope of this topic, the general principles of fetal heart tracing evaluation are applicable. A category 1 tracing denotes a reassuring fetal status, where fetal acidemia is unlikely to be present; however, it does not rule out abruption. A category 2 fetal heart tracing is indeterminate and may require additional evaluation strategies. In contrast, a category 3 fetal heart tracing indicates a high likelihood of fetal acidemia, suggesting that delivery is indicated if the category 3 tracing does not resolve with resuscitative measures. The presence of a sinusoidal pattern is concerning for fetal anemia, which can result from abruption. [16]

content: Blood work—including a type and screen, complete blood count, clotting studies (fibrinogen, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time), and blood urea nitrogen—provides baseline parameters to evaluate changes in patient status. The Kleihauer-Betke test may be ordered to detect fetal blood cells in maternal circulation. This test does not diagnose the presence of placental abruption but quantifies the presence of fetal blood in the maternal circulation. This knowledge is particularly essential in Rh-negative patients, as the mixing of fetal blood in the maternal circulation can lead to isoimmunization. Therefore, if a significant fetal-maternal bleed is present, the Kleihauer-Betke test results help to determine the needed dose of Rh (D) immune globulin to prevent isoimmunization.

title: Placental Abruption -- Treatment / Management
content: The onset of placental abruption is often unexpected, sudden, and intense, and requires immediate evaluation. Prehospital care for a patient with a suspected placental abruption should involve advanced life support and transport to a hospital with a full-service obstetrical unit and a neonatal intensive care unit. Upon arrival at the hospital, most patients receive intravenous fluids, supplemental oxygen, and continuous maternal and fetal monitoring (when indicated by gestational age) while the history and physical examination are performed. Subsequent treatment varies based on the data collected during the assessment, the gestation of the pregnancy, and the degree of distress experienced by the patient or the fetus. [17] [18]

title: Placental Abruption -- Treatment / Management
content: Patients classified with class 1 (mild) placental abruption, no signs of maternal or fetal distress, and a pregnancy earlier than 37 weeks of gestation may be treated conservatively. These patients are typically admitted to the obstetrical unit for close monitoring of maternal and fetal status. Intravenous access and blood work for type and cross-match are part of the care plan. The maternal-fetal dyad continues to be monitored until there is a change in condition or fetal maturity. In clinically stable patients with mild placental abruption, outpatient management with close follow-up may be a suitable option. Follow-up care typically includes frequent prenatal care visits and antenatal testing, which may include non-stress tests and/or biophysical profiles. Growth ultrasounds should be obtained serially, as placental abruption is associated with an increased risk of fetal growth restriction.

title: Placental Abruption -- Treatment / Management
content: The decision for delivery is dependent on an assessment of maternal and fetal status, and includes consideration of factors such as the pregnant patient's hemodynamic stability, the fetus's gestational age, and fetal viability. If fetal demise is diagnosed, immediate delivery is recommended. Otherwise, delivery is typically necessary if the collected data results in class 2 (moderate) or class 3 (severe) classification and the fetus is viable and alive. Because of hypertonic contractions, a vaginal birth may occur rapidly. Given the potential for coagulopathy, vaginal birth often presents less risk to the mother. However, if there are signs of fetal distress or rapid maternal decompensation, an emergency cesarean birth may be necessary. Careful management of fluids and circulatory volume is vital during labor or a surgical procedure. Postpartum, the patient needs to be monitored for postpartum hemorrhage and alterations in the clotting profile. A neonatal team must be in the delivery room to receive and manage the infant. The neonatal team should be informed of the concern for placental abruption, as maternal-fetal hemorrhage can lead to anemia in the fetus.

title: Placental Abruption -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Pathogenic bleeding in later pregnancy is most commonly caused by placental abruption; however, other etiologies—particularly placenta previa—should also be considered. Differentiating these 2 conditions is vital to the patient's care. The information below compares the presentation of placental abruption and placenta previa on common parameters included in an obstetrical examination. Bleeding may be visible or concealed with placental abruption, and is external and visible with placenta previa. The degree of anemia or shock may be greater than the visible blood loss in placental abruption and is equal to that in placenta previa. Pain may be intense and acute in cases of placental abruption, and is unrelated to placenta previa. The uterine tone is firm and board-like in placental abruption and soft and relaxed in placenta previa.

title: Placental Abruption -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Cervical changes associated with labor may also cause vaginal bleeding. Labor is suspected in a patient with a smaller amount of vaginal bleeding, symptoms consistent with contractions (but not the constant, intense pain often associated with placental abruption), and evidence of cervical shortening or dilation on digital examination.

title: Placental Abruption -- Prognosis
content: Prognosis depends on multiple factors, including the amount of bleeding associated with the abruption, the degree of maternal and fetal compromise, and gestational age at delivery. Partial placental separation is associated with lower mortality compared to complete separation. There is a risk of maternal and fetal mortality with placental abruption, particularly in cases where hemodynamic compromise is present. Placental abruption accounts for 10% to 20% of maternal deaths. [7]

title: Placental Abruption -- Complications
content: The complications associated with placental abruption are as follows: Maternal death Fetal demise Severe hemorrhage Coagulopathy Hysterectomy Transfusion-associated complications Delivering a premature infant Possible need for cesarean section Fetal growth restriction Recurrence has been reported in 4% to 12% of cases.

title: Placental Abruption -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Deterrence and patient education are vital components in reducing the incidence and severity of placental abruption. Educating patients about the warning signs—such as sudden abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, uterine tenderness, and decreased fetal movement—empowers them to seek immediate evaluation, which can be lifesaving. For patients with a history of placental abruption, counseling on the elevated risk of recurrence is essential for informed decision-making in future pregnancies. Additionally, addressing modifiable risk factors plays a key role in prevention. Patients should be encouraged to manage conditions such as uncontrolled hypertension through regular prenatal care, medication adherence, and lifestyle changes, and to avoid substance use such as cocaine, which increases risk. Through clear education and proactive deterrence strategies, clinicians can help patients recognize early warning signs, take preventive measures, and engage in timely care, ultimately improving outcomes for both mother and fetus.

title: Placental Abruption -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Placental abruption is a serious pregnancy complication that is best managed by an interprofessional team of healthcare professionals, including, but not limited to, an obstetrician, obstetric nurse, obstetric anesthesiologist, neonatologist, and adult intensivist (if intensive care is required). Diagnosis and skilled assessment are crucial in placental abruption, as a wide range of presentations exists. Patients may present with minimal bleeding, no hemodynamic compromise, and can be expectantly managed; they can also present very dramatically with maternal and fetal compromise and require urgent intervention.

title: Placental Abruption -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: The triage team must promptly recognize placental abruption and immediately begin a thorough evaluation of maternal and fetal status. Resuscitation should begin without delay, and the obstetrician must be notified as soon as possible. If significant hemodynamic instability or coagulopathy is present, the intensive care team should also be activated. Blood should be typed and cross-matched, and the facility's massive transfusion protocol should be initiated as needed. The obstetric anesthesia team should be alerted promptly, and the operating room should be prepared. Although urgent cesarean delivery is not required in all cases, it may be necessary in situations of rapid maternal deterioration or significant fetal compromise. The neonatal intensive care unit team should also be notified to ensure readiness. A coordinated, interprofessional approach is essential to reduce the morbidity and mortality associated with placental abruption, optimizing outcomes for both the patient and fetus.

title: Placental Abruption -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: While placental abruption cannot be prevented in all cases, modifiable risk factors should be addressed. Smoking cessation and avoidance of cocaine should be encouraged. Some patients may benefit from drug counseling and or drug rehabilitation. [19] For patients with chronic hypertension, active treatment of hypertension during pregnancy has been shown to decrease the incidence of placental abruption. [20] [21]

title: Placental Abruption -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Placental abruption is a serious, potentially life-threatening condition for both the pregnant individual and the fetus. Complete or near-complete separation of the placenta typically results in fetal death unless delivery occurs immediately. Reported fetal mortality rates range from 1% to 40%, depending on gestational age and the severity of the abruption. In the United States, placental abruption accounts for approximately 1% to 5% of maternal deaths annually. Beyond hemorrhage, associated morbidities include the need for blood transfusions, complications from prematurity, hysterectomy, and cesarean delivery, which may increase the likelihood of cesarean births in future pregnancies. Recurrence rates range from 3% to 10%, underscoring the importance of careful monitoring and management in subsequent pregnancies. [2] [22]
